title: AI notetaker tl;dv left 181,874 meeting records queryable by any logged-in user
subtitle: A missing Firestore tenant-isolation rule turned an AI-transcription service used by more than two million people into a searchable index of other customers' video calls — including live sessions, government meetings, and roughly a thousand recordings streaming at any moment.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Independent security researcher bobdahacker publicly disclosed on August 15 that tl;dv, an AI-transcription service that joins Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams calls to produce searchable notes, exposed 181,874 meeting records belonging to 84,312 users across 35,003 email domains. The Firestore collection holding meeting metadata was missing a rule restricting reads to the record's own organization — meaning any authenticated tl;dv user could query the collection and pull other customers' call titles, participants, transcripts, and active conference IDs. Roughly one thousand meetings were streaming at any given moment during the window the flaw was open.

The timeline is the ugly part. The researcher reported the vulnerability to tl;dv on January 28, 2026. It remained open through July. Dark Reading confirmed on August 4 that the exposure was still live at press time, and the researcher's own August 15 write-up notes that fixes were only pushed after public disclosure — nearly seven months after private notification. Exposed conference IDs during the open period were sufficient for a stranger to join active calls, which affected corporate accounts, universities, and dozens of government agencies that had adopted tl;dv as a productivity tool.

The pattern is now familiar. Every AI notetaker sits between a video-conferencing session and cloud storage, which means every one is a high-value target with the same failure mode: a permissions rule missing on a shared datastore turns tenant isolation into a fiction. Otter, Fireflies, and Read.ai have all faced adjacent scrutiny in 2026; the tl;dv disclosure lands in the same month as the Hugging Face breach post-mortem and the encrypted-reasoning-trace attacks, and together they mark AI middleware as the current soft edge of the enterprise stack.

Takeaway for learners: assume every AI tool that joins your meetings is a data-broker in disguise, and audit accordingly. Before adopting a notetaker at work, ask three questions — where the recordings live, what tenant-isolation guarantees the vendor makes at the database layer, and how quickly they patched their last publicly disclosed flaw. If any of those answers are vague, treat the tool as a channel that leaks whatever gets said on the call.
